subject: robotGardener
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: rusty robot gardener.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I need to plan out a full module carefully. I'm weighing stylistic directions for the rusty robot gardener concept, considering unexpected choices like folk-art tin-toy lithograph or botanical Art Nouveau styling rather than the obvious steampunk/Wall-E look.

Settling on a vintage seed-packet lithograph aesthetic: cream paper, halftone dots, bold ink outlines, a limited six-ink palette of rust orange, teal, mustard, cream, and deep navy, with flat printed shading and decal-style text like "SEEDS." Now I'm sketching the robot's physical design: a barrel-torso humanoid about 1.7m tall with a straw hat, apron, watering can, trowel, flowers sprouting from a chest cavity pot, ivy on the arm, and rust textures mottled across the surface.

I'm working out the rig structure (hips, spine, chest, neck, jaw, limbs down to fingers and toes) and a readable A-pose rest stance, then deciding how to incorporate gardening tools—trowel, watering can, tool belt with shears—without breaking the pose too much, landing on a straw hat, bibbed apron with seed packet decal, and tools hanging from a belt or hand.

Simplifying the watering solution into a backpack tank with a hose running to a nozzle holstered at the hip, freeing the right hand for a trowel and the left hand for a small daisy, and adding charming growth touches like ivy on the forearm or a sunflower poking through the hat.

For the chest, I like replacing the heart with a little glowing seedling in a glass-fronted box, giving the character a soft green glow at its core. The eyes could be round decal lenses with a halftone seed-packet pattern, glowing amber, with one eye intentionally dimmer or cracked for character.

Now I'm sketching out the full skeleton proportions — roughly 1.75m tall, with hip, spine, and neck joints stacked vertically, legs running from hip through knee to ankle with boxy boots resting at ground level, and arms extending from shoulders through elbows to wrists in an A-pose.

I'm computing the arm joint positions using angle and length math, then working out finger joints for each hand as small chains of base-mid-tip points to keep the hand detailed but within the joint budget.

For box section sweeps, radius is just half the box extents. For the held items in rest pose, I'll just place the daisy stem through the palm region, running a rod from above down through the fingers so it looks naturally gripped.

Let me reconsider the finger curl—fingers point downward and curve slightly forward, so a stem running along that forward axis would get wrapped by the curled fingers near the front of the palm, which feels more natural than trying to align it with the finger axis itself.

Actually, a simpler approach: rather than fight with a gripped stem, I could just tuck the item into a tool belt instead.

Now I'm thinking through the rest of the pose — open relaxed hands with dirt-stained fingertips for a cleaner rig, a hat with a daisy tucked in the band, trowel holstered at the belt, and a watering backpack with hose and nozzle holstered at the hip.

Setting up the ink color palette...

Writing halftone paint shader logic...

Going with 2048 texels for safety margin on the dot pattern. Now I'm writing the halftone paint function that projects onto the dominant axis, computes shading from the light direction, and builds a 45-degree rotated dot grid with radius driven by shade intensity.

Still defining paint layers...

I'm generalizing ink mixing by resolving the base color and blending it with the ink tone. For edge definition, I'll skip view-dependent outlines and instead rely on ink-colored seams and thick black separation gaps between parts to create the misregistration effect.

I'm also considering importing the clockwork kit for mechanical gear details—placing a gear train on the robot's cheek using the flat style, plus small gears at each knee, trusting the kit's bone-parenting options to handle placement.

I'm giving the head gears spin joints so they rotate, keeping other gears static, and tinting them rusty copper tones to match the halftone palette while staying consistent with the gear texture's multiply-tint system.

For the ~200 part target, I'm planning a mirroring loop over left/right sides, and standardizing joint-local positions using the word-based `{left, up, forward}` form instead of raw coordinate arrays for clarity and consistency across the model.

Actually, simplifying further, I'll just work in explicit model-space coordinates everywhere instead of relative joint offsets, and define helper box/cylinder functions for the blocky robot parts.

Still writing helper functions...

Now I'm thinking through the torso shape—considering whether to loft it along a spine chain or just build it as a simple frustum of boxes, leaning toward the simpler chunky barrel approach.

Mapping out the body parts attached to bones: a pelvis box on the hips, a ribbed accordion-style cylinder for the abdomen on the spine, and a tapered frustum box for the chest. I'm also sketching the skeleton hierarchy, starting with the hips root and a catmull spline spine chain running upward.

I'm sketching overall body proportions — torso, neck, and head heights, aiming for a chunky stylized robot gardener around 2 meters tall with a big head and straw hat. Still working out the joint coordinates for the spine chain, deciding where hips, spine1, and spine2 (chest) should sit.

Writing bone definitions...

For the head, I'm planning a box roughly 0.34 wide, 0.30 tall, and 0.30 deep centered around y=1.80, with the cranium and jaw as separate pieces.

Working out the jaw joint position and dimensions so the lower jaw box sits just under the head, overlapping slightly with the neck in a way that stays hidden since it functions as a chin plate.

I'll settle the neck top at y 1.65 with the jaw box spanning 1.64–1.71, letting a small hidden overlap exist near the base where it won't be visible. I'm overthinking the fine joint details, so I decide to commit to a compact but rich build targeting roughly 250 parts and 700-800 lines, using loops to generate repeated parts efficiently. I'll define a head center constant and start planning out 5-8 textures to use across the model.

I'm sketching out the texture list: amber ring-lens eyes (big and small/cracked), a seed packet decal, ivy leaf and daisy/sunflower flower cards, a glowing seedling window for the chest, stenciled name plaques, grass blade cards, and reusing the gauge texture from the clockwork for the backpack tank -- landing around nine textures total. Then I work through eye placement, deciding to use textured planes slightly offset from the head surface, torus rings for goggle rims lying flat in the front plane, and dark cylinder sockets, considering whether the goggles should sit raised on top of the head.

Still refining geometry...

For the hat itself, I'm positioning it atop the head with a slight downward sink and tilting it rakishly via the lathe axis parameter, then adding a ribbon band at the crown base as a thin lathed torus-like shape in a rust color to contrast the mustard straw.

Now I'm thinking through how a sunflower stalk could push up through a hole in the hat's crown, emerging from the top of the head.

I need to confirm how card orientation works: the card lies in the plane defined by the facing axis and width, facing along the flow direction, so with frame pointing up along the stem and flow set to +Z, the sunflower card should stand upright facing forward.

Since a card's bottom edge sits on its frame, I'll place the flower drawing so its base aligns with the top of the stalk, using a sunflower illustration sized around [0.22, 0.22]. Since the card is thin edge-on from the side, I should consider adding a second copy visible from that angle too.

For the hat band I'll add small daisy cards, and for ivy I'm thinking of sweeping vine paths around the arm and torso with leaf cards placed along the path using tangent-aligned frames so the leaves stick outward naturally.

With lean around 60 and varied flow, the leaves splay nicely around the vine to sell the ivy look. Now I'm deciding the vine's sweep route, planning to wrap it along one leg and up through the opposite arm.

Working out the spiral math for the leg wrap...

Setting kneeL as the bone for the vine attachment, so the vine leaves travel along that joint's path. I need to use `b.along` to get placement frames for the vine cards, passing a count and a callback — I'll use a no-op callback since the return value is what I actually need.

For the arm vine, I'm working out a spiral wrap around the upper arm axis using a perpendicular vector computed via cross product, so I can build a reusable helper that wraps a vine around any center/axis with a given radius, turn count, and length.

For the legs, I'm planning a chain structure—hip to knee to ankle—built with named bones under the hip parent, then using tapered box frustums between joints to give the thighs and shins a boxy, robotic tapered look rather than smooth tube sweeps.

Still defining the leg chain...

Now I'm setting up the arm chain: shoulderL, elbowL, wristL as a 3-point polyline with role "arm", deciding to skip a separate clavicle joint for simplicity. For the upper arm, I'm using a frustumBox between shoulder and elbow tilted along its axis, and thinking through how the box orientation should follow that tilted axis correctly.

I'm considering using faceted rod geometry (octagonal, 8 sides, flat shading) for the limbs to give them a tube-like robotic look, and planning half-dome pauldrons on the shoulders using a partial sphere geometry rotated to face upward and outward in rust color.

For the hands, I'm figuring out a palm box shape with three fingers plus a thumb, computing the forearm direction vector from elbow to wrist to orient the hand correctly, then deriving a hand-pointing direction so I can place finger bases extending from the wrist along that vector.

Working through the finger spread now: positioning the three fingers along the z-axis with slight gaps while the thumb sits forward and angled outward, keeping the palm oriented inward toward the body for a natural relaxed hand pose.

Settling on two joint names per finger segment since that matches the span count without a tip joint, treating each as a "digit" chain parented to the wrist joint, and sweeping with a faceted hexagonal cross-section for a boxy look.

For the fingertips, I'm thinking of adding dirt-stained coloring using a band gradient near the tips, combining a base color with bands that split the finger sweep so the last stretch reads as soiled.

Now I'm tallying up the total joint count across hips, spine, neck, arms, fingers, legs, toes, and extra gear joints to confirm it stays under the limit, then starting on the torso's rigid parts, beginning with the pelvis box dimensions.

Still designing the torso parts...

Layering the window frame as nested boxes, with a mustard rim, ink-dark inset, and a glowing seedling texture plane positioned just in front, skipping transparency since materials stay opaque.

Now I'm adding the apron: a cream canvas bib panel extruded from the chest downward.

I'll add a pocket overlay with a seed packet decal, skip the bib idea since it conflicts with the chest window, and go with a half-apron using waist ties instead. For the fabric look I'm writing a custom paint helper that generates a cream canvas with woven grid lines combined with halftone shading, using a fixed light direction to compute surface darkness.

Still writing the halftone dot math...

I need to check whether the agentic-3js-builder SDK actually exports all these helper names like resolve, mix, noise, smoothstep, and the Paint/ColorInput types before relying on them in my import statement.

Now I'm defining a limited ink palette with hex values for colors like navy, teal, rust, mustard, and leaf green, then layering mottled textures to build a "rusty" paint effect by combining base and darker rust tones with noise parameters.

Defining rust and teal paint functions...

Still defining paints...

Now I'm laying out the full build plan in order: skeleton first, then legs and boots with knee gear and vine, pelvis and belt with tool pouches, the torso with its windowed chest panel and rivets and stencil decal, shoulders, collar, the back-mounted watering tank with straps, gauge and hose, then the neck, and finally the head with skull, face plate, goggles, glowing eyes, and mouth grille.

I'm continuing with the jaw, antennae-ears with a gear train, and a sunflower-and-daisy hat, followed by arms, hands, glove cuffs, vines with leaves, a small flower tucked in the belt, trowel, shears, and grass-tuft moss cards on the shoulders and hat. For the rivets, I'm planning to merge small sphere geometries into a single mesh per group using BufferGeometryUtils, with a helper function that places rows of rivets along given points on a bone.

Now I'm working out the back tank placement: a vertical cylinder behind the chest with mustard torus rings as bands, a domed cap on top, a filler cap, a gauge plane facing backward on the tank, a pump handle rod on the side, and strap boxes running from the tank over the shoulders to the chest front.

I'm also tracing a hose path with catmull-rom curve points from the tank's side down to a nozzle holster at the right hip, swept with a small radius and a dark teal ink color, ending in a brass cone-and-cylinder nozzle attached to the hip bone.

I'm checking the hose clears the thigh and arm geometry in the A-pose, confirming the coordinates don't intersect. Then I'm adding a tool belt setup around the hips: a trowel holster on the right side, shears on the left, and seed pouches mounted in front, plus starting on the face decal with horizontal slots for the mouth grille.

For the mouth grille I'm building small boxes forming vertical slits across the lower jaw front face in mustard with a friendly, smile-like shape, adding rivets, leaf-shaped eyebrow details in rust, and pink blush circles printed on the cheeks for a touch of character.

For the ears, I'm setting up small gear trains on each side of the head, placing paired gears with different tooth counts and spoke styles that spin as linked joints, giving the robot a mechanical, playful detail.

Flat face style will rely on texture names, that's fine, and the right-side axle just flips the axis direction. Just two gears meshed together, no overlap issues to worry about.

For elbows and knees I'll skip double-gear trains and just place single flat gears with no spokes, module 0.006, positioned at the outer joint face with axis along [s,0,0], letting the arbor default to its standard cylinder.

Now I'm shifting to the eye/lens design: concentric circles forming a navy outer ring, amber and orange iris bands with radial spoke lines, a navy pupil with cream highlights, and a ring of small halftone dots for texture, then adding a glow effect on top of it.

I'm also sketching the seedling window (teal background with a glowing leaf sprout and tiny sun), a seed-packet apron pocket with cream background, navy border, bold serif "SEEDS" text and a flower illustration, plus a small chest plate stencil reading something like "UNIT 7 · GARDENER" or "No.7 GARDEN". Now I'm starting on an ivy leaf texture with a lobed shape, visible veins, layered greens, and a navy outline.

Next I'm designing a daisy texture with eight cream petals rotated around a mustard center and navy outlines, planning a pink variant for vines and belt flowers, with stems included in the card so they work on the hat sprout too. Then I move on to sketching a sunflower texture with large petals.

I'm sketching out the scattered decorative elements: grass tufts and moss patches as small card textures placed on the shoulders and pauldron, plus thinking through how to attach the pauldron dome to the shoulder bone so it follows arm rotation properly, including a small ball joint sphere at the connection point.

Working through torso measurements to make sure the shoulder sphere, chest box, and neck collar dimensions all line up proportionally, then planning a collar ring with rivets and a trapezoidal shoulder yoke plate transitioning from the wider chest top down to the narrower neck opening.

For the chest, I'm adding small panel details and cylindrical valve knobs near the window, keeping the back mostly plain since it's hidden by the tank. For the abdomen, I'm spacing out a few accordion-style rings between the pelvis top and chest bottom to fill that gap.

Now I'm blocking out the pelvis as a simple box positioned at the hip joint, then building the legs from rod-shaped thigh and shin segments with sphere knee joints and mustard-colored bands, plus a small armor plate on the shin front.

Working through the boot geometry, making sure the ankle ball joint and boot mesh overlap properly so the foot sits flush at ground level without gaps between the shin, ankle, and toe box. Now I'm moving on to positioning the hand.

Setting up imports for the scene builder, pulling in geometry utilities and the kit modules for clockwork gears and glow effects, but I need to double-check that every export actually comes from the single builder module as required rather than scattered across kit submodules.

Writing helper functions for boxes and cylinders...

Spheres work fine for basic shapes too. For rivets, I'm merging multiple small sphere geometries at different translated positions into a single mesh to reduce draw calls, using low-poly spheres for efficiency.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton hierarchy, starting with the hips joint as the root with a spine role, then building a spine chain from a polyline of three points, which creates two spans and needs two intermediate joint names.

Continuing with the neck chain parented to the chest joint, then defining the head joint at the neck's tip with its own orientation and role.

Then I'm adding a jaw joint attached to the head, aimed forward, and setting up a loop that builds mirrored leg chains for left and right sides with hip, knee, and ankle joints along a polyline from the hips down.

Adding toe joints and arm chains...

Still placing the finger positions...

Working out finger geometry and color palette for the glove segments...

Now I'm sketching the head: skull box dimensions and position, then a faceplate panel in front where the goggles will attach, trying to settle on a cream-colored plate.

Still working out layering...

Placing eye planes just inside the goggle torus openings, scaling the right eye slightly smaller for asymmetry, then shaping small rust-colored leaf brows positioned above the goggles but below the head's top curve.

For the face details, I'm adding pink blush circles on the cheeks (keeping it flat rather than textured dots to save complexity) and a small mustard-colored cylindrical rivet nose centered below the eyes.

Now I'm mapping out the mouth grille as a mustard plate below the goggles, checking that the vertical regions for goggles, nose, mouth, and jaw don't overlap awkwardly — the nose placement is slightly colliding with the goggles' inner edges, so I need to nudge it.

Let me restructure the skull geometry: skull spans y 1.73–2.0 with the face plate centered at y=1.855, goggles centered at y=1.885 with radius .065 (so 1.82–1.95), a mouth slot at y=1.785 with small teeth boxes, and a lower jaw block centered at y=1.70 running in depth from z=0 to .24.

I'm positioning the jaw box (0.30 × 0.07 × 0.22) slightly forward of the face plate, with its hinge around (0, 1.70, 0.0), and a neck cylinder (radius .07, height .16) tucked underneath so it stays hidden beneath the head and jaw. I'm adding thin vertical grille slots on the jaw front as small ink-colored boxes.

For the antennae, I'm considering a rod topped with a pink flower bulb near the head's upper-left, but since the hat brim (radius .31) would swallow it, I'm deciding to skip the antenna and instead let a sunflower stalk emerge through a hole in the hat. For the ears, I'm placing small gear-train discs at ±0.19 radius .054 on each side, and sketching headphone-style cups as short radial cylinders.

Now I'm working out the hat geometry — crown radius .13 versus the head's half-width of .18, figuring out whether the crown sits fully inside the head box or needs to drop lower so the hat visually wraps around the head rather than perching awkwardly on top.

Tilting the hat back slightly so the brim clears the goggles instead of shading them — checking that a tilt of about 12° on the axis lifts the front edge enough. I'll set the crown radius to .20, height .16, brim .36, positioned just above the head with a slight backward tilt so it sits naturally without blocking the face.

Verifying the brim covers the ear gear at the sides without clipping it, and that the hat profile (crown walls tapering into the brim) sits correctly relative to the head's top surface. Now I'm placing the sunflower stalk coming off the top of the hat, accounting for the tilt axis so it angles slightly backward too.

I'm checking that the sunflower card height doesn't push the total figure past 2.5m — the current size is too tall, so I'm scaling down the flower and stalk dimensions to fit.

I'll finalize the flower stalk/card dimensions and skip adding a sunflower-daisy pair, keeping just the sunflower. For the hat, I'm adding small pink daisy accents tucked along the hat band using outward-facing frames at a few crown positions, plus a lathed ring for the band itself with a contrasting stripe color.

I'm settling on a reddish-pink hue matching the daisies for the ribbon, and confirming the band radius sits cleanly within the crown wall. For the straw texture I'm using a grain function to give the hat a woven look, skipping any extra wear details for simplicity.

Now I'm moving to the torso, laying out the pelvis as a teal box and adding a belt box just above it.

For the leather tones I'm adding a mottled brown texture and a brown ink accent, plus a mustard belt buckle with an inset detail. I'm shaping the apron as an extruded scalloped outline hanging from the hips, and carefully adjusting the z-depth so the belt sits in front of the apron without clipping — nudging their positions until the layering reads correctly.

Now I'm designing the apron pocket as a pointed-bottom rectangle with a seed-packet label stuck on top, tilted slightly for a natural roll, and considering whether to add stitching detail or an ink outline behind the pocket by scaling the outline shape outward around its centroid.

I'm checking the ink backing layer's thickness and z-offset against the apron's front faces to make sure the rim shows without z-fighting, and the belt pouches work out even though they overlap slightly with the thighs. Then I'm placing tool holsters on each hip, with a trowel handle rising from the right pouch and shears planned for the left.

Now I'm routing the hose from the tank base down to a nozzle hanging at the back-right hip, building the nozzle as a simple cylinder-and-cone shape pointing downward. Then I'm moving on to the torso parts: the chest box with rust variation toward the bottom, a top frustum plate, a rim plate underneath, and starting on a window assembly on the front face.

Still laying out window dimensions and rivets...

Adding rust side patches for texture, mustard dial knobs with tiny ink needles flanking the collar, and starting on shoulder straps.

I'm also considering ivy details on the chest and placing a mustard collar ring with gasket neck details, then working out the back tank geometry and its mounting brackets.

Still working out colors—settling on a rust tank body with mustard or teal accent bands to contrast against the main plating.

Still adding tank details...

I'll place the gauge near the neck back on the left side, facing outward with a brass bezel cylinder, so it reads clearly from that angle. On the right side I'll add a matching stencil-style label plate, like an "AQUA" decal in navy and cream, facing the opposite direction for symmetry.

Now I'm working out the shoulder straps as a curved path over the top plate, using a small rectangular cross-section for thickness, colored brown like bone. I'll skip adding a gear train on the back since the tank covers that area, but I'll keep an upper-back plate visible from the sides, and start positioning an exhaust pipe on the left.

Next I'm routing a ribbed hose from the tank bottom down behind the pelvis to the hip, giving it a teal rubber color with brass couplers at each end, and capping it with a small mustard-colored nozzle cylinder.

Then I'm checking the hose doesn't collide with the right arm's position, adding a ribbed neck with steel cylinder segments and rust-dark rings at a few heights, and moving on to the shoulders.

For the shoulders, I'm placing a ball joint sphere and a pauldron dome with a mustard rim ring sitting on top of the arm bone, positioning the dome center above the shoulder point and considering tilting it outward by rotating about the z-axis to match the arm's outward angle.

I'm also planning moss tufts on the pauldron tops, calculating the dome's surface height at offset positions so the tufts sit flush on the curved top, sinking slightly into the surface for a natural look.

Instead of manually computing hit points, I realize I can use a surface scatter function directly on the dome part to generate scattered points filtered to upward-facing normals, then feed those hits into the card generator for grass-like tufts with some lean, bend, and random variation. This approach is more robust since the surface scatter handles the dome's curved geometry automatically within the bone's local frame.

For the elbow joint, I'm placing a small sphere with a flat gear disc on its outer face—sizing the gear radius and module, skipping spokes since the rim styling should hold visually, and assigning it to the elbow bone. I'm planning the color scheme next: teal for the upper arm rods tapering from shoulder to elbow, with rust-dark forearms and mustard cuff rings to tie the joints together.

Now I'm continuing the forearm with a thinner rust-colored rod, then adding a wrist cuff cylinder oriented along the forearm's direction vector, followed by a palm box and knuckle rivets for the hand. For decoration, I'm sketching out vine placements—spiraling up the left leg and left forearm bones, with a smaller ivy creep on the right boot—and thinking through how to generate leaf-card frames along those vine paths using a helper that walks the curve and invokes a callback at each point.

I'm adding leaf cards along the vine frames with varied size, lean, and flow direction, plus occasional flower cards every few frames, and tuning the ivy's sweep radius and polygon sides. Finally I'm making sure the whole figure rests properly on the ground by checking that the boot soles sit at y=0.

Now I'm designing the eye textures as seed-packet style SVGs: a healthy left eye and a dim, cracked right eye, each built from navy rims, cream rings, radiating spokes, and a dotted border pattern.

For differentiation, I want heterochromatic irises—amber for the left eye, a dimmer teal-green for the right—with a crack motif drawn as jagged lines across the right eye to suggest damage.

Now for the seedling texture, I'm designing a dark navy-teal background with rounded corners, halftone sun rays, and a small sprout growing from a soil mound with a green stem and layered leaves, plus glowing cream light motes scattered around for atmosphere. Next I'm sketching the packet texture with a cream backdrop.

Still planning textures...

Now I'm designing the tank label with a water drop icon and "H2O" text, plus the gauge textures for the pressure dial and chest knobs, working out their placement coordinates relative to the chest windows.

I could add moss cards on the hat brim and a flower sticker decal on the chest.
